newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Oil drilling to resume in Albania this week.
newsitem.headline: Oil drilling to resume in Albania this week.

text.p: Croatian oil company Ina-Naftaplin said on Tuesday it planned to resume onshore drilling in Albania this week after suspending operations in March amid violent unrest in the Balkan nation.

State-owned Ina-Naftaplin is the only oil company currently drilling in Albania and its onshore well at Peze, halfway along the 40 km stretch between Tirana and the port of Durres, is being viewed as a test project by other oil companies.

Crude oil output in Albania has plummeted over the past decade, with annual production of 488,000 tonnes from four state-owned fields in 1996 compared to between 2-2.5 million tonnes in the early 1980s and 845,000 tonnes in 1991.
Ina-Naftaplin's technical operating manager Zdenko Dvorscak said the armed uprising in Albania, triggered by the collapse of fraudulent investment funds, had cost the company.
"Financially we have suffered," Dvorscak told Reuters in a interview at Ina-Naftaplin's office in central Tirana.
Ina-Naftaplin started drilling at Peze, one of its two onshore concessions, last August, contracting the equipment from the United States through Croatian owned service company, Crosco.

But after the government declared a state of emergency on March 2, Ina-Naftaplin suspended operations temporarily, evacuated 53 staff from the country, and on March 13 declared a force majeure which reduced costs on equipment.
"We are now planning to start up again on May 1 and hope to eliminate the force majeure on May 10," Dvorscak said.
"We are close to finishing although we had some trouble at the well...but we hope to reach the target of about 5,000-5,200 metres in the month of May."
Dvorscak said his company has so far spent about $10 million on the well after spending around $5 million on seismic and other preparatory work.
"My calculation is now that this suspension will add another $2.5 million on to the project," he said.

Ina-Naftaplin is one of a list of oil exploration companies that have moved into Albania since the fall of communism in 1990, tempted by the state's onshore production in the 1980s and lured by the 380 km of spectacular Adriatic coastline.
International oil groups are estimated to have invested over $150 million in oil/gas exploration in Albania since 1990.
Austrian oil group OMV is in final negotiations on three onshore blocks and was hoping to drill at one of these but this work was now not likely to proceed until next year.
This block is jointly owned with OMV holding 40 percent, Britain's Enterprise Oil Plc 30 percent, Clyde Petroleum Plc 15 percent and Hungary's MOL 15 percent.
OMV is also involved offshore, last year drilling a well in a joint venture with U.S. group Occidental Petroleum Corp.
The well was found dry and abandoned. Occidental pulled out and OMV now wholly owns the block, which is one of five blocks offshore Albania.
Occidental drilled a deep water well at its wholly owned offshore block, Adriatiku 3, halfway between Albania and Italy, two years ago but it was also dry.
The company, which is also in final negotiations for three onshore blocks, said it had found quite positive geological data and planned to drill another well this autumn.
"We contracted the rig 18 months ago and all the supplies are in place in Brindisi (Italy)," company president Jerry Williams told Reuters by telephone from Colorado.
"These plans have not been altered at all although it may be delayed a bit, by a month."
Italian company Agip SpA finished drilling at an offshore block in late March, finding nothing, but still has interests in several onshore blocks.
British oil company Premier Oil drilled a deep onshore well of 6,000 metres in 1995 in a joint venture with government petroleum company Albpetrol but without finding oil.
Albpetrol has also signed an agreement with Fountain Oil of the U.S. to drill a well on an existing onshore field.
Chevron was present in Albania for several years but has now left the country while Royal Dutch/ Shell Group has two onshore concessions but has not started work.
"Everyone is watching our well," said Dvorscak. "If we find oil I think we will see a big boom in Albania, particularly if the political situation is stabilised."
